headline: Healey's first Budget doubles the bank surcharge and scraps gas standing charges

terms.meaning: An extra tax on bank profits, on top of normal corporation tax.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent body that forecasts the public finances.
A fixed daily fee on an energy bill, charged however much energy you use.

levels.headline: Healey's first Budget doubles the bank surcharge and scraps gas standing charges
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget on 28 October 2026. The Bank Corporation Tax Surcharge will rise temporarily from 3% to 6% between 1 January 2027 and 31 March 2028, below the 8% some reports had predicted.
The money helps pay for energy support. A £2.6 billion Household Energy Payment will put £100 into bank accounts from January 2027 for households in England in council tax bands A to D, covering up to 20 million homes. Standing charges on household gas bills are being abolished, and the devolved governments receive their shares through the Barnett formula.
The Office for Budget Responsibility raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.2% but expects 1.0% in 2027, with inflation peaking at 3.8% in early 2027. Debt is forecast to reach 83.8% of GDP next year before falling, and the OBR confirmed the government meets its fiscal rules.
levels.why: It shows who pays for help with energy bills and whether the government can keep borrowing under control.

levels.headline: Healey raises the bank surcharge to pay for energy bill help
levels.body:
In his first Budget on 28 October, Chancellor John Healey announced a temporary rise in the bank surcharge from 3% to 6%, running from 1 January 2027 to 31 March 2028. Pre-Budget reports had suggested 8%.
The package includes a £2.6 billion Household Energy Payment of £100, paid from January 2027 to households in England in council tax bands A to D. Standing charges on gas bills will be scrapped. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland get their share under the Barnett formula.
The independent Office for Budget Responsibility now expects growth of 1.2% this year and 1.0% in 2027, and inflation peaking at 3.8% in the first quarter of 2027. It says debt will rise to 83.8% of GDP next year before falling, and that the government is meeting its fiscal rules.
levels.why: The Budget decides which groups pay more tax and which get support during a period of high energy costs.

levels.headline: Budget doubles the bank surcharge to fund £100 energy payments
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey used his first Budget, on 28 October, to raise the surcharge on bank profits from 3% to 6% for just over a year, from January 2027 to the end of March 2028. That is lower than the 8% many had expected.
The government will use the money to help with energy costs. Households in England in council tax bands A to D, up to 20 million of them, will get £100 from January 2027, at a cost of £2.6 billion. Standing charges, the fixed daily fee on gas bills, will be abolished.
The official forecaster, the OBR, expects the economy to grow 1.2% this year and 1.0% next year. It says inflation will peak at 3.8% early in 2027 and that the government is keeping to its borrowing rules.
levels.why: Energy bills are a big worry for families, and banks are being asked to help cover the cost.

levels.headline: Chancellor taxes banks more to help with energy bills
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey set out his first Budget on 28 October. Banks will pay a higher surcharge on their profits, rising from 3% to 6% from January 2027 until March 2028. Some reports had expected it to go as high as 8%.
The extra money helps pay for support with energy bills. About 20 million households in England in council tax bands A to D will get a £100 payment from January 2027, costing £2.6 billion. The fixed daily standing charge on gas bills will also be removed.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, which gives independent forecasts, thinks the economy will grow by 1.2% this year and 1.0% in 2027. It expects prices to rise fastest, at 3.8% a year, early in 2027, and says the government is following its own borrowing rules.
levels.why: It affects what households pay for energy and how much banks pay in tax.

levels.headline: The Budget asks banks to pay more and gives households £100 towards energy
levels.body:
On 28 October the Chancellor, John Healey, announced his first Budget. Banks will pay a bigger extra tax on their profits for about fifteen months: the surcharge goes from 3% to 6% between January 2027 and March 2028.
Part of the money pays for a £100 payment to households in England in council tax bands A to D, which are the lower-value homes. Up to 20 million households could get it from January 2027. The government is also ending standing charges on gas bills. A standing charge is a fixed daily fee that you pay even if you use no gas.
The independent forecaster, the OBR, expects the economy to grow by 1.2% this year. It also expects prices to keep rising faster than usual until early 2027, peaking at 3.8%.
levels.why: It could lower household bills this winter, while asking banks to carry some of the cost.

levels.headline: Banks will pay more tax, and households will get help with energy bills
levels.body:
The government has published its Budget, which is its yearly plan for taxes and spending. The Chancellor, John Healey, announced it on 28 October.
Banks will pay more tax on their profits. An extra charge on them goes up from 3% to 6% from January 2027 until March 2028. The government will use some of that money to help people pay for energy. Homes in England in council tax bands A to D, which are the lower-priced homes, will get £100 from January 2027. That could help up to 20 million households. Gas bills will also lose the standing charge, a daily fee that stays the same however much gas you use.
Independent experts at the OBR think the economy will grow a little this year and next. They expect prices to rise fastest in early 2027.
levels.why: It helps ordinary families with winter bills, and shows how governments pay for that help.

levels.headline: Banks pay more tax so families can get help with energy bills
levels.body:
Every year the government explains its plans for taxes and spending. This is called the Budget. The Chancellor, John Healey, gave this year's on 28 October.
Banks will have to pay more tax on their profits for a while. The extra tax will double, from 3% to 6%, between January 2027 and March 2028. The government will use some of the money to help with energy bills. Lots of homes in England, up to 20 million, will get £100 in January 2027. Gas bills will also stop having a standing charge. That is a fixed fee you pay every day, even when you use no gas.
A group of independent experts called the OBR checks the sums. It thinks prices will keep going up quite fast until early 2027.
levels.why: It means some families get cash to help pay the heating bill this winter.

levels.headline: The government will take more tax from banks to help people pay for energy
levels.body:
The Chancellor is the person who looks after the country's money. His name is John Healey. On 28 October he told Parliament how the government will collect and spend money. This plan is called the Budget.
Banks make a lot of profit, and they already pay a bit of extra tax. That extra tax will double for about a year and a half. The government will use some of it to help with energy bills. Many families in England will get £100 in January. Gas bills will also lose a daily fee that people used to pay even if they used no gas.
A team of experts checks the plan. They think prices will keep rising faster than we would like until early next year.
levels.why: Some families will have a bit more money to heat their homes.

levels.headline: The government is asking banks to pay more so families can pay less for energy
levels.body:
Imagine your school needs money for a new playground. The grown-ups decide the biggest businesses should chip in a bit more. That is a little like what the government has just done.
The man in charge of the country's money is called the Chancellor, and his name is John Healey. He has said that banks must pay more tax for a while. Some of that money will help families pay for gas and electricity. Lots of families in England will get £100 in January. Gas bills will also lose a fixed daily fee.
Some experts have checked the plan. They think prices will keep going up a bit faster than usual until early next year.
levels.why: It is a way of sharing the cost of heating homes, so families do not have to carry it alone.

levels.headline: Banks will chip in so families get help with heating
levels.body:
Think of a school bake sale. Everyone gives a little so the class can pay for something nice. The grown-ups in charge of the country have done something like that.
They said that banks, which look after people's money, must pay a bit more. Then some families will get £100 to help pay for heating. Heating keeps houses warm when it is cold, so this is a kind thing.
It is also a bit like pocket money. A country has only so much, so the grown-ups have to choose carefully who gets it. They also check that they are not spending more than they can afford, so there are no nasty surprises later.
levels.why: The grown-ups share out money so more families can stay warm.

headline: US stocks close higher for a third straight day after the Fed holds rates

terms.meaning: An index tracking 500 of the largest companies listed in the US.
An index dominated by technology companies.
An index of 30 big US companies.

levels.headline: US stocks close higher for a third straight day after the Fed holds rates
levels.body:
US stocks closed higher on Wednesday 28 October, the last completed trading session, for a third straight day. The S&P 500 rose 0.28% to close at 7,743.98. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 97.53 points, or 0.19%, to 52,475.10, and the Nasdaq Composite added 0.27% to 26,549.85.
The rise followed the Federal Reserve's decision to leave interest rates unchanged at 3.75% to 4%. Two policymakers wanted a quarter-point increase, which markets read as a sign that rate rises could return.
Oil prices also moved higher that day, and investors are weighing higher borrowing costs against steady company earnings. Trading Economics reported a slightly different Dow close of about 52,509, so the exact figure varies by source.
levels.why: Share prices reflect confidence about the economy and affect pensions and savings.

levels.headline: Wall Street extends its winning run to three days as the Fed stands pat
levels.body:
US shares finished higher on Wednesday 28 October, the latest completed session, marking a third consecutive daily gain. The S&P 500 was up 0.28% at 7,743.98, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.19% to 52,475.10, and the Nasdaq Composite advanced 0.27% to 26,549.85.
Investors had been waiting for the Federal Reserve, which held its policy rate at 3.75% to 4%. Two members voted for a quarter-point rise, and traders now expect the Fed may raise rates before the end of the year.
The gains were modest. Higher oil prices and the chance of more expensive borrowing are still worries, even though the main indices remain close to record territory. Other data providers show slightly different Dow figures.
levels.why: Markets show how investors judge interest rates and inflation, which feed through to savers and borrowers.

levels.headline: S&P 500, Dow and Nasdaq all rise for a third day after the Fed holds rates
levels.body:
On Wednesday 28 October, the last full trading day, the main US stock indices all rose for the third session in a row. The S&P 500, which tracks 500 big companies, gained 0.28% to finish at 7,743.98. The Dow, made up of 30 large companies, rose 0.19% to 52,475.10. The Nasdaq Composite, which leans towards technology, climbed 0.27% to 26,549.85.
The moves came after the Federal Reserve kept its interest rate at 3.75% to 4%. Two of its decision makers would have preferred a small increase. That suggests rates could go up later.
The daily gains were small. Investors are still keeping an eye on oil prices and inflation.
levels.why: Share prices affect pension funds and savings, so they matter beyond Wall Street.

levels.headline: US shares rise again after the Federal Reserve keeps interest rates the same
levels.body:
US stock markets ended higher on Wednesday 28 October, which was the most recent full day of trading. It was the third day in a row of gains. The S&P 500 index, which follows 500 of America's biggest companies, rose 0.28% to 7,743.98. The Dow Jones index went up 0.19% to 52,475.10, and the Nasdaq, packed with technology firms, went up 0.27% to 26,549.85.
The good mood followed news that the Federal Reserve, America's central bank, did not change interest rates. Two of its members wanted a small rise, so traders think a rise might come before long.
The rises were small, so this is a steady day rather than a big jump.
levels.why: Shares reflect how confident investors feel, which can affect pensions and jobs.

levels.headline: American shares go up for the third day running
levels.body:
Shares in big American companies went up again on Wednesday 28 October. This was the last full day of trading, and it was the third rise in a row. Experts follow three main lists of company shares. The S&P 500 rose 0.28% to 7,743.98. The Dow rose 0.19% to 52,475.10. The Nasdaq, which has lots of technology firms, rose 0.27% to 26,549.85.
The rises came after the US central bank, the Federal Reserve, said it would leave interest rates where they are. Two of its leaders wanted a small increase, so more rises could come later.
The changes were small, so there was no big excitement.
levels.why: Share prices show how people feel about the economy, and many pensions are invested in them.

levels.headline: US share prices edge up again after rates are left alone
levels.body:
A stock market is a place where people buy and sell small pieces of companies, called shares. In America, share prices went up on Wednesday 28 October. It was the third rise in a row.
People track share prices using lists called indexes. The S&P 500 follows 500 big companies. It went up by 0.28% to 7,743.98. The Dow follows 30 big companies and went up 0.19% to 52,475.10. The Nasdaq, which has lots of technology firms, went up 0.27% to 26,549.85.
The US central bank, the Fed, kept its interest rate the same. Interest rate is the price of borrowing money. Two Fed leaders wanted it to go up a little. The rises in share prices were small.
levels.why: Many pension savings are invested in shares, so rising prices can help ordinary savers.

levels.headline: US shares go up a little for the third day in a row
levels.body:
Companies sell tiny pieces of themselves, called shares. People buy them, hoping the shares will be worth more later. On Wednesday 28 October, American share prices went up a little for the third day running.
There are lists that show how shares are doing. The S&P 500 list has 500 big companies, and it went up by 0.28%. The Dow list has 30 companies, and it went up 0.19%. The Nasdaq list has lots of technology companies, and it went up 0.27%. That is less than one penny in every pound.
The US bank in charge of money, the Fed, did not change interest rates. Interest is the extra money you pay when you borrow. People think it might go up soon.
levels.why: Many people's savings are tied up in shares, so small moves matter.

levels.headline: American shares rose a little for a third day
levels.body:
Think of shares as tiny slices of a big pizza company. If lots of people want a slice, the price goes up. This week, the prices of many American company slices went up for the third day in a row.
People keep score with lists. One list follows 500 big companies. It rose by 0.28%, which is a very small step up. Another follows 30 big companies and rose 0.19%. A third has lots of computer and phone companies, and it rose 0.27%.
The people in charge of America's money decided not to change the cost of borrowing. Two of them wanted it to go up a bit. So the grown-ups are watching to see what happens next.
levels.why: It tells us that investors feel fairly calm, and that matters for savings and jobs.

levels.headline: Share prices in America crept up for a third day
levels.body:
Imagine a school fair where you can swap tickets for little pieces of the stalls. If lots of people want a piece, the price rises. That is a bit like shares. In America, the prices of lots of shares rose a little on Wednesday for the third day in a row.
Grown-ups follow lists of shares to see how the whole market is doing. One list of 500 big companies went up by about a quarter of one penny in every pound. Another list of 30 firms, and one with lots of technology firms, also went up a tiny bit.
America's bank for banks left the price of borrowing money alone. Two of its leaders wanted it to rise slightly.
levels.why: It shows people feel steady about money, which helps keep jobs and savings safe.

levels.headline: Share prices in America went up a tiny bit again
levels.body:
Some people own tiny pieces of big companies. These pieces are called shares. When the company does well, the pieces can be worth more.
This week the price of lots of pieces in America went up a tiny bit, for the third day running. It was only a small step, like growing a tiny bit taller.
The people in charge of America's money decided not to change anything this time. That kept people calm. Some of them still think the cost of borrowing money might go up soon, so everybody is watching carefully, like a class waiting to hear what the teacher will say next.
levels.why: Many grown-ups keep their savings in shares, so small changes matter to them.

headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% in September, driven by fuel, and rate rise bets grow

terms.meaning: The rate at which prices rise over time.
Inflation leaving out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco.
The Bank of England's interest rate, which influences loan and savings rates.

levels.headline: UK inflation rises to 3.5% in September, driven by fuel, and rate rise bets grow
levels.body:
UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in the 12 months to September 2026, up from 3.1% in August, the Office for National Statistics reported on 21 October. Economists polled by Reuters had expected 3.4%.
Motor fuel prices were the main driver. Core inflation, which excludes energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was 2.8%, services inflation was 3.7%, goods inflation reached 3.2%, its highest since September 2023, and CPIH, which includes housing costs, was 3.6%.
The Bank of England's Bank Rate stands at 3.75%. In September three of nine policymakers voted for a rise to 4%, and markets widely expect an increase at the next meeting on 5 November. Some traders price two rises by the end of the year. The next inflation figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: Higher inflation squeezes household budgets and makes higher interest rates more likely.

levels.headline: Inflation jumps to 3.5% as fuel costs bite, strengthening the case for a rate rise
levels.body:
Annual consumer price inflation reached 3.5% in September 2026, compared with 3.1% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics. Forecasters had expected 3.4%. The ONS published the figures on 21 October.
Rising motor fuel costs were the main cause. Core inflation was 2.8% and services inflation 3.7%, while goods inflation reached 3.2%, the highest since September 2023.
The Bank of England holds Bank Rate at 3.75%, and three of nine members voted for a rise in September. Markets widely expect the Bank to raise rates on 5 November, and some traders expect two rises by the end of the year. The next ONS inflation release is on 18 November.
levels.why: It decides how far prices keep rising and whether mortgages and loans get dearer.

levels.headline: UK inflation climbs to 3.5% because of higher fuel prices
levels.body:
Prices in the UK were 3.5% higher in September than a year earlier, the Office for National Statistics said on 21 October. In August the figure was 3.1%. Economists had expected 3.4%.
The biggest reason was the cost of petrol and diesel. Core inflation, which leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, was lower at 2.8%. Prices of services rose 3.7%, and prices of goods rose 3.2%, the fastest since 2023.
The Bank of England sets interest rates to keep inflation under control. Its rate is 3.75%, and many people think it will go up on 5 November. Some traders think there could be two rises before the end of the year. The next figures are due on 18 November.
levels.why: Rising prices and rising interest rates both change what people can afford.

levels.headline: Prices are rising faster again, mostly because of fuel
levels.body:
The cost of living went up faster in September. The Office for National Statistics said prices were 3.5% higher than a year before, compared with 3.1% in August. Experts had guessed 3.4%.
The main cause was more expensive petrol and diesel. A different measure of inflation, called core inflation, leaves out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco. It was 2.8%. The cost of services such as haircuts and train tickets rose 3.7%, and the cost of goods rose 3.2%.
The Bank of England sets the main interest rate, which is 3.75%. Many experts think it will raise the rate on 5 November to slow price rises. Some think two rises could come by the end of the year. The next figures arrive on 18 November.
levels.why: It affects the price of your shopping, and the cost of a mortgage or loan.

levels.headline: Prices rose faster in September, mainly because petrol and diesel cost more
levels.body:
Inflation is the speed at which prices go up. In September it was 3.5%, which means a typical basket of shopping cost 3.5% more than a year earlier. In August the rate was 3.1%. This was a bit higher than experts had expected.
Most of the rise came from fuel. Petrol and diesel cost more. If you take out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, the number is lower, at 2.8%. This is called core inflation. Things you pay for as a service, such as haircuts, rose 3.7%.
The Bank of England can raise its interest rate to slow prices down. It is now 3.75%, and many people think it will rise on 5 November. The next price figures come out on 18 November.
levels.why: Higher prices mean your money buys less, and higher rates make borrowing cost more.

levels.headline: Prices are going up faster, mostly because fuel costs more
levels.body:
Inflation means prices going up over time. In September the rate was 3.5%. That means something that cost £100 a year ago now costs about £103.50. In August the rate was 3.1%, so prices have sped up.
Most of the extra rise came from petrol and diesel. If you leave out energy, food, alcohol and tobacco, prices rose by less, 2.8%. The cost of services like haircuts went up 3.7%.
The Bank of England is in charge of interest rates. Interest is the price of borrowing money. Right now it is 3.75%. When prices rise too fast, the Bank can make borrowing dearer so people spend less. Many experts think it will do that on 5 November.
levels.why: If prices rise faster than wages, families can afford less.

levels.headline: Shop prices are rising a bit faster, mostly because fuel costs more
levels.body:
When prices go up over the year, that is called inflation. A year ago, a toy might have cost £100. Now the same toy might cost £103.50. That is what 3.5% means. It was 3.1% last month, so prices are speeding up.
The main reason is that petrol and diesel cost more. Take away energy and food, and prices went up less.
The Bank of England looks after interest rates. Interest is the extra money you pay back when you borrow. The Bank can make it higher to slow rising prices. The rate is 3.75% now, and many people think the Bank will raise it on 5 November.
When prices go up and wages do not, families can buy less.
levels.why: It affects how far a family's money goes each week.

levels.headline: Prices in shops went up a bit faster last month
levels.body:
Prices change over time, and usually they go up a little. Last month they went up faster than before. Experts say prices are now 3.5% higher than a year ago. If a sweet cost £1 last year, it might cost about 3 or 4 pence more now.
A big reason is that petrol and diesel cost more. Cars and lorries need fuel, and when fuel is dear many other things become dear too.
There is a bank called the Bank of England. It looks after the cost of borrowing money, called the interest rate. If prices rise too quickly, the bank can make borrowing cost more. Many people think it will do this soon.
levels.why: When things cost more, families need to be careful with their pocket money and wages.

levels.headline: Things cost a little more than before, mostly because of fuel
levels.body:
Think about your favourite sweet. Last year it cost £1. Now it might cost 3 or 4 pence more. When lots of things cost a bit more than last year, grown-ups call it inflation.
It has sped up. A big reason is that petrol and diesel cost more. Lorries and cars need them to bring things to the shops, so lots of other things cost more too.
There is a special bank for the whole country, called the Bank of England. It is like the boss of the banks. It can make borrowing money cost more, which helps stop prices rising so fast. Lots of people think it will do that soon.
levels.why: When prices rise, the coins in your pocket buy a little less.

levels.headline: Things in shops cost a little more than before
levels.body:
Imagine a packet of sweets that cost £1 last year. Now it costs a few pennies more. When lots of things cost a bit more, grown-ups call it inflation.
Prices went up a little faster last month. A big reason was that petrol and diesel cost more. Lorries and cars need them to carry things to the shops, so lots of other things cost more too.
There is a big bank for the whole country. It can make borrowing money cost more, which helps stop prices rising so quickly. Many grown-ups think it might do that soon, so they are watching closely.
levels.why: When prices rise, the coins in your pocket buy a little less.

headline: UK brings forward its defence spending target to 2030 and unveils a £10 billion Ukraine package

terms.meaning: A military alliance of countries, including the UK, that defend each other.
The government body that backs loans and insurance for exports.
A promise that the World Bank will cover a loan if it is not repaid.

levels.headline: UK brings forward its defence spending target to 2030 and unveils a £10 billion Ukraine package
levels.body:
In the 28 October Budget, Chancellor John Healey set 2030 as the date for UK defence spending to reach 3% of GDP, and reaffirmed the NATO goal of 3.5% by 2035. Details are due at next year's spending review.
The government called its Ukraine package the largest ever. It includes £7 billion of economic support over three years, with up to £5.5 billion of World Bank guarantees and a £500 million grant to the World Bank's crisis facility. A further £500 million will fund air defences this winter, and UK Export Finance capacity for Ukraine rises by £3 billion to £6.5 billion, mainly for military support.
The National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will put up to £5 billion over four years into defence and dual-use technology. One analyst said the plans lacked detail.
levels.why: It sets how much of the UK's money goes to defence and to supporting Ukraine.

levels.headline: Healey pulls forward the 3% defence target and pledges record support for Ukraine
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey told MPs on 28 October that defence spending will reach 3% of GDP by 2030, and that the NATO target of 3.5% by 2035 stands. He said the plan to meet these targets will be set out at next year's spending review.
The Ukraine package includes £7 billion of economic support over three years, using up to £5.5 billion of World Bank guarantees. There is £500 million for air defences this winter and a £3 billion rise in UK Export Finance capacity, bringing the total to £6.5 billion. This sits on top of the £3 billion a year already committed.
Up to £5 billion from public investment bodies will go into defence technology. An analyst said the announcement lacked detail.
levels.why: The decisions will shape the UK's defence budget and its role in supporting Ukraine.

levels.headline: UK sets 2030 for 3% defence spending and announces its largest Ukraine package
levels.body:
Chancellor John Healey said in the Budget on 28 October that the UK will spend 3% of national income on defence by 2030. He also repeated the UK's promise to NATO to reach 3.5% by 2035. How the money will be found will be explained at next year's spending review.
The government also announced what it calls its biggest ever support for Ukraine. This includes £7 billion of economic help over three years, £500 million for air defences this winter, and £3 billion more capacity for loans and insurance backing exports, mainly for military support. This is on top of £3 billion a year already promised.
A further £5 billion over four years will go into defence technology. One analyst said the plan lacked detail.
levels.why: It affects taxes and spending, and the UK's place alongside its allies.

levels.headline: The UK will spend more on defence sooner and give Ukraine a bigger support package
levels.body:
The Chancellor, John Healey, said in the Budget on 28 October that the UK will spend 3% of what the country earns on defence by 2030. The UK has also promised its NATO allies it will reach 3.5% by 2035. The government will explain next year how it plans to pay for this.
The UK also announced its biggest ever package for Ukraine. It includes £7 billion in help for Ukraine's economy over three years and £500 million for air defences this winter. The government is also widening its backing for loans and insurance to Ukraine by £3 billion, mainly for military items. It already gives £3 billion a year.
Some £5 billion will also go into defence technology. One expert said there was little detail.
levels.why: Defence spending competes with other things the government could spend money on, like health and schools.

levels.headline: The UK promises to spend more on defence and help Ukraine more
levels.body:
The government's chief money minister, called the Chancellor, is John Healey. On 28 October he said the UK will spend 3% of everything the country earns on its defence by 2030. That is sooner than planned. The UK has also promised its friends in NATO, an alliance of countries who protect each other, to reach 3.5% by 2035.
He also announced the UK's biggest ever help for Ukraine, which is fighting a war with Russia. That includes £7 billion over three years to help Ukraine's economy and £500 million for air defences this winter. Air defences are systems that stop missiles and drones.
Some extra money will go into defence technology. One expert said more details are needed.
levels.why: It shows how the UK balances paying for defence with paying for everything else.

levels.headline: The UK will spend more on defence sooner, and send big help to Ukraine
levels.body:
The government has to decide how to use the country's money. One thing it spends on is defence, which means the army, navy and air force. On 28 October, the Chancellor, John Healey, said defence spending will rise to 3% of what the country earns by 2030. That is sooner than before.
The UK also said it will give Ukraine its biggest ever help. Ukraine is a country that was attacked by Russia. The UK will give £7 billion over three years to help keep Ukraine's economy running. It will also give £500 million for air defences, which protect against missiles and drones.
The plan does not yet say exactly where all the money comes from. That will be explained next year.
levels.why: It matters because defence costs a lot, and the money must come from taxes or borrowing.

levels.headline: The UK will spend more to protect itself and to help Ukraine
levels.body:
Countries pay for armies and equipment to keep people safe. This is called defence. On 28 October, the person in charge of the UK's money, John Healey, said the UK will spend more on defence. By 2030 it will use 3 pence of every pound the country earns on it.
The UK is also helping Ukraine, a country that has been in a war. It will give much more help than before, including £7 billion over three years for its economy and £500 million to defend against missiles and drones.
Grown-ups still need to explain exactly how the UK will find all this money. That will happen next year.
levels.why: Money spent on defence cannot be spent on other things, so leaders must choose.

levels.headline: The UK says it will spend more on keeping safe and will help Ukraine
levels.body:
Every country has to decide how much to spend on keeping its people safe. This is called defence. The UK's money boss, called the Chancellor, said the UK will spend more on it. By 2030, three pence of every pound the country earns will go on defence.
The UK also wants to help a country called Ukraine, which has been fighting in a war. It is giving a very big amount of help. Some pays to keep Ukraine's shops and schools running. Some pays for equipment to stop missiles.
But the money has to come from somewhere. The grown-ups will explain how next year.
levels.why: Spending on one thing means less for another, so these choices matter to everyone.

levels.headline: The UK will spend more to keep people safe and will help Ukraine
levels.body:
Imagine your class has a pot of money for the year. You can spend it on books, games or a trip. Countries have a big pot too, and they must choose. On 28 October the UK said it will spend more on defence, which is the army, navy and air force that keep people safe.
The UK will also help Ukraine, a country in a war. It will send lots of money to help families there and to buy things that stop missiles.
There is only one pot, though. If more goes to defence, less may be left for other things. The grown-ups will explain next year how they will manage it.
levels.why: Like a class pot of money, a country's budget has to be shared carefully.

levels.headline: The UK will spend more on staying safe and on helping a friend
levels.body:
Imagine you have a jar of money for the whole year. You must choose between books, games and a trip. A country has a big jar like this too, and it must choose carefully.
This week the UK said it will put more of its money into defence. Defence means the people and the equipment that keep us safe.
The UK also wants to help Ukraine, a country that is in a war. So it will give a lot of money to help people there. The grown-ups will explain next year how they will pay for it all, because the jar can only hold so much.
levels.why: A country's jar of money is limited, so leaders must choose what matters most.

headline: Oil rises to about $115 a barrel after a reported Houthi strike on a Saudi refinery

terms.meaning: The main international benchmark price for oil.
West Texas Intermediate, the main US oil price benchmark.
An Iran-aligned armed group in Yemen.

levels.headline: Oil rises to about $115 a barrel after a reported Houthi strike on a Saudi refinery
levels.body:
Brent crude futures rose 1.3% to settle at $115.32 a barrel on Wednesday 28 October, while US West Texas Intermediate gained 2.9% to $102.78. Prices were near six-month highs.
Two things drove the rise. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, which handles 550,000 barrels a day, with a ballistic missile. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike. Separately, reports said the US had told Gulf countries to prepare for renewed strikes on Iran after the 3 November midterm elections.
On Thursday Brent slipped 82 cents to $114.50 as hopes of peace talks offset supply fears. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan have held talks with Iranian officials. Iran has also stepped up attacks on tankers in the Gulf this month.
levels.why: Oil prices feed into petrol, heating and inflation around the world.

levels.headline: Brent near $115 as Saudi refinery attack and Iran strike reports stoke supply fears
levels.body:
Brent crude settled at $115.32 a barrel on Wednesday 28 October, up 1.3%, and US benchmark WTI closed at $102.78, up 2.9%, leaving both near six-month highs.
The Houthi movement said it had struck Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery, a 550,000 barrel a day facility, with a ballistic missile. Riyadh did not immediately confirm that. Reports also said Washington had told Gulf states to prepare for new strikes on Iran after the 3 November midterms.
Brent eased 0.7% on Thursday to $114.50 as diplomacy offered some hope. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan held talks in Tehran, and the US Vice President reportedly sent a letter to Iran's security chief. Iran has attacked tankers in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz this month.
levels.why: Energy prices push up inflation and affect interest rates.

levels.headline: Oil climbs to about $115 as the Middle East conflict threatens supplies
levels.body:
The price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, closed at $115.32 a barrel on Wednesday 28 October, up 1.3%. US crude closed at $102.78, up 2.9%. Both are near six-month highs.
The rise followed claims by the Houthis, an Iran-backed group in Yemen, that they had hit Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery, Ras Tanura, with a missile. Saudi Arabia has not immediately confirmed this. There were also reports that the US had told Gulf countries to prepare for fresh strikes on Iran after the 3 November midterm elections.
On Thursday the price slipped slightly to $114.50 because of hopes for peace talks. Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan met Iranian officials in Tehran. Iran has also been attacking oil tankers.
levels.why: More expensive oil makes petrol, heating and many goods cost more.

levels.headline: Oil prices jump because of attacks and worries about war with Iran
levels.body:
The price of oil rose on Wednesday 28 October. Brent, the main world price, finished at $115.32 a barrel. The American price finished at $102.78. Both are close to their highest for six months.
Two news stories pushed prices up. A group in Yemen called the Houthis, which is backed by Iran, said it hit Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery with a missile. Saudi Arabia had not confirmed this. Reports also said the US told countries in the Gulf to get ready for new strikes on Iran after elections on 3 November.
On Thursday the price dipped a little, to $114.50, as people hoped for peace talks. Iran has been attacking oil tankers this month.
levels.why: Oil prices change what you pay for petrol and heating.

levels.headline: Oil gets more expensive after an attack on a Saudi oil site
levels.body:
Oil is what we turn into petrol and diesel. On Wednesday 28 October the price of oil went up again. A barrel of the main international kind, called Brent, cost $115.32. That is close to the highest price in six months.
There are two reasons. A group in Yemen, called the Houthis, said it hit one of Saudi Arabia's biggest oil refineries with a missile. A refinery is a factory that turns oil into fuel. Saudi Arabia did not at first say whether this was true. Also, people said the US might attack Iran again after elections on 3 November.
On Thursday the price dipped a little because people hope for peace talks.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol and heating can cost more as well.

levels.headline: Oil prices go up as fighting in the Middle East worries buyers
levels.body:
Oil is dug from the ground and made into fuel for cars, lorries and planes. When something might stop the oil flowing, the price goes up. This happened on Wednesday 28 October. A barrel of the main world kind, called Brent, cost $115.32. That is almost the highest in six months.
A group in Yemen called the Houthis said it hit a big oil factory, a refinery, in Saudi Arabia with a missile. Saudi Arabia did not at first say if that was true. People also said the US could attack Iran after elections on 3 November.
The next day the price fell a tiny bit. Some countries were talking to Iran to try to keep the peace.
levels.why: Dearer oil can make petrol, heating and food cost more.

levels.headline: Oil costs more because of fighting in the Middle East
levels.body:
Oil is a thick liquid from under the ground. We use it to make petrol and diesel. If people worry that there will be less oil, they pay more for it. That is what happened this week.
A barrel of Brent, the oil that sets the main world price, cost about $115. That is close to its highest price for six months. A group called the Houthis, who live in Yemen, said they hit a Saudi Arabian oil factory with a missile. Saudi Arabia had not yet said if that was true. People also said the US might attack Iran after an election on 3 November.
Some countries are trying to talk to Iran to keep the peace.
levels.why: If oil costs more, it costs more to drive, heat homes and move goods.

levels.headline: Oil is more expensive because of trouble in the Middle East
levels.body:
Cars, buses and lorries need fuel. Fuel is made from oil. When people think there might be less oil, shops and companies pay more for it. That happened this week.
A group of fighters in Yemen said they hit a big oil factory in Saudi Arabia. A country far away, Iran, might also be attacked by the US after an election. People worry that fighting could stop oil getting to the places that need it. So a barrel of oil now costs about $115, close to the highest in six months.
The next day the price fell a little, because some countries were having talks to try to keep the peace.
levels.why: If oil is dear, many things from petrol to toys can cost a bit more.

levels.headline: Oil costs more because of fighting far away
levels.body:
Think of oil as the juice that makes cars, buses and planes go. If there is a problem and the juice might run low, the price goes up. This week there was trouble in the Middle East, a part of the world where a lot of oil comes from.
Some fighters said they hit a big oil factory. People also worried about more fighting with a country called Iran. So the price of oil went up to about $115 for a barrel. A barrel is a big drum, bigger than you!
Then some countries began talking to Iran to try to keep the peace, and the price dipped a little. Grown-ups are watching closely.
levels.why: It can make petrol and the things we buy cost more for families.

levels.headline: Oil costs more because there is trouble far away
levels.body:
Cars and buses need fuel to go. Fuel is made from oil. Oil comes out of the ground, and lots of it comes from a part of the world called the Middle East.
This week there was trouble there. Some fighters said they hit a place that makes fuel. People also worried about more fighting. When people think there might be less oil, they are ready to pay more for it, a bit like children swapping stickers.
So oil now costs more. Later the price dipped a little, because some countries are talking to try to keep the peace. Grown-ups are watching closely.
levels.why: When oil costs more, petrol and many other things can cost more too.

headline: Israel election leaves Netanyahu and his rival short of a majority

terms.meaning: Israel's parliament, which has 120 seats.
A survey of voters as they leave polling stations, used to predict results.
A government made of several parties working together.

levels.headline: Israel election leaves Netanyahu and his rival short of a majority
levels.body:
Israel held a general election on 27 October, its first since the 7 October attacks. Exit polls from major TV stations suggested Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc won about 50 seats, the opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot 52 to 53, and Arab parties 17 to 18, in the 120-seat Knesset. Neither side reached the 61 needed for a majority.
Likud was projected as the largest party with 24 to 25 seats. Eisenkot declared victory and said he should get the first chance to form a government, though he said in the campaign he would not govern with Arab lawmakers. Turnout was 77.7%, the highest in 27 years. Partial counts differed from the exit polls, and official results are due on 4 November. Analysts say Netanyahu could stay in office for months.
levels.why: The coalition talks will decide who leads Israel during tensions with Iran and the war in Gaza.

levels.headline: No clear winner in Israel as exit polls show both blocs short of 61 seats
levels.body:
Exit polls after Israel's 27 October election put Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc on about 50 seats, the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot on 52 to 53, and Arab parties on 17 to 18. Parliament has 120 seats, so 61 are needed.
Likud was the largest party on 24 to 25 seats. Eisenkot, a former military chief, claimed victory and said he should have the first chance to form a government. During the campaign he said he would not govern with Arab lawmakers, who might instead back a minority government from outside.
Turnout was 77.7%, a 27-year high. Early partial counts differed from the exit polls, so the picture may change. Official results are due on 4 November, and analysts expect Netanyahu could remain in office for months.
levels.why: The result shapes Israeli policy on Gaza and Iran.

levels.headline: Israel's election ends without a clear majority for either side
levels.body:
Israelis voted on 27 October in their first general election since the attacks of 7 October. Exit polls suggest nobody won a majority in the 120-seat parliament. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc was put on about 50 seats, the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot on 52 to 53, and Arab parties on 17 to 18. A government needs 61.
Likud looks to be the biggest single party. Eisenkot, a former army chief, has said he won and should get first go at forming a government, though he ruled out working with Arab parties. They might support a minority government from outside.
Turnout was 77.7%, the highest in 27 years. Official results come on 4 November, and talks could take months.
levels.why: Who governs Israel will affect the war in Gaza and tensions with Iran.

levels.headline: Israel's election has no clear winner, early results suggest
levels.body:
People in Israel voted on 27 October. It was the first national election since the attacks of 7 October. Polls taken as people left the voting stations suggest that neither side won enough seats to rule alone. Parliament has 120 seats, and a group needs 61.
The exit polls gave Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's group about 50 seats. The opposition, led by Gadi Eisenkot, got 52 or 53. Arab parties got 17 or 18. Eisenkot, a former army chief, said he had won, but he has said he will not work with Arab parties.
More people voted than in any election for 27 years. Official results are due on 4 November. Netanyahu could stay in power for months while parties talk.
levels.why: The next government will make big decisions about war and peace in the region.

levels.headline: Nobody has clearly won Israel's election
levels.body:
People in Israel voted for a new parliament on 27 October. The parliament is called the Knesset and it has 120 seats. A group needs 61 seats to run the government on its own side. Early guesses, made by asking voters as they left, say that nobody got there.
The leader of the country, Benjamin Netanyahu, and his friends were guessed to win about 50 seats. The other side, led by Gadi Eisenkot, was guessed at 52 or 53. Arab parties were guessed at 17 or 18. Eisenkot says he won, but he says he will not work with the Arab parties.
More people voted than in any election for 27 years. The official results are due on 4 November.
levels.why: It decides who leads a country that is dealing with war and tension.

levels.headline: Israel's election has no clear winner yet
levels.body:
Israel has a parliament called the Knesset, with 120 seats. People voted for it on 27 October. To lead the country, a group needs more than half the seats, which is 61.
People asked voters as they left the voting places. The answers suggest that nobody has 61. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's side may have about 50. The other side, led by Gadi Eisenkot, may have 52 or 53. Arab parties may have 17 or 18. A smaller party cannot decide alone, so groups must now talk and try to join together. This kind of team is called a coalition.
The official results are due on 4 November. The talks could last for months.
levels.why: The people who lead Israel make decisions that affect the whole region.

levels.headline: Israel voted, but no side won enough seats
levels.body:
Israel held an election on 27 October. In an election, people choose who will make the rules for their country. Israel's group of lawmakers is called the Knesset. It has 120 seats, so you need 61 to have the most.
When people left the voting places, they were asked how they voted. The answers suggest that neither big group got 61 seats. It is like a class vote where nobody gets over half the votes. The groups now have to try to work together to form a team called a coalition.
The official count is due on 4 November. The talking could take many months.
levels.why: The leaders chosen will make choices about war and peace.

levels.headline: Israel had an election, but nobody clearly won
levels.body:
An election is when people vote to choose their leaders. Israel had one on 27 October. The leaders sit in a place called the Knesset, which has 120 seats. To win, a group needs 61 seats, which is more than half.
Imagine your class voting for a new class rule. If two groups each get less than half, nobody wins by themselves. They have to talk and agree to work together. That seems to be what has happened in Israel.
The official numbers will come on 4 November. Then the groups will talk. This could take months, so for now the old leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, stays in his job.
levels.why: Leaders have to work together, and that can take time.

levels.headline: Israel voted for its leaders, but there is no clear winner yet
levels.body:
Choosing leaders is like choosing a class captain. In Israel, people did this on 27 October. But instead of one captain, they chose a big group of 120 people who make the rules.
If a team gets 61 of the 120, it can lead. Early guesses say no team got that many. It is like a class vote where neither captain got more than half of the votes.
So the teams must now talk and try to join up. That could take a long time. The person who was leader before, Benjamin Netanyahu, will probably stay in the job for now.
levels.why: When no one wins clearly, leaders must work together to get anything done.

levels.headline: Nobody has clearly won the vote in Israel
levels.body:
Imagine your class votes for a new class captain. Two children each get fewer than half of the votes. Nobody has clearly won. That is a bit like what happened in Israel.
People there voted for the leaders who help run their country. The early counts say that no group got more than half. So the groups must now talk to each other. They try to join up into one big team.
This can take a very long time. For now, the person who was already the leader will probably stay in the job. The proper count is due on 4 November.
levels.why: Leaders who work together can make decisions for a whole country.

headline: At least 68 dead after two high-speed trains collide in Spain

terms.meaning: Spain's state railway operator.
A private high-speed rail operator in Spain.
Days of national remembrance declared by a government.

levels.headline: At least 68 dead after two high-speed trains collide in Spain
levels.body:
Two high-speed trains collided near Urda in Toledo province on 28 October, killing at least 68 people, according to the Castilla-La Mancha regional government. More than 100 people were reported injured, and health services said 15 of 53 treated were in a serious condition.
A Renfe train and an Iryo train were involved on the Madrid to Seville line. Iryo said its train was struck from behind. Transport Minister Óscar Puente said the control system at Urda failed and six trains were stopped, and one was allowed to restart and travelled 25 kilometres before hitting a stopped train at high speed. An order from the control centre is being investigated, and the cause is not confirmed.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared three days of official mourning and promised a tough line on any safety failures. It is Spain's second deadly high-speed crash this year.
levels.why: It raises serious questions about rail safety in Spain, and the investigation may change how trains are controlled.

levels.headline: Spain's second deadly high-speed rail crash this year leaves at least 68 dead
levels.body:
At least 68 people died when two high-speed trains collided near Urda, in Toledo province, on 28 October, the regional government said. More than 100 people were reported hurt, and the toll could rise. Earlier reports had given lower figures.
The trains were operated by Renfe and Iryo on the Madrid to Seville line. According to Transport Minister Óscar Puente, the control system at Urda failed, six trains were halted, and one was allowed to restart and covered 25 kilometres before hitting a stationary train at speed. Euronews reports that officials point to human error after a computer failure, and an "inexplicable" control centre order is being investigated.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced three days of mourning and vowed to be tough on any safety failings.
levels.why: Investigators' findings could lead to changes in how Spain runs its rail network.

levels.headline: At least 68 killed in a train collision in Spain
levels.body:
Two high-speed trains crashed into each other near the town of Urda, in Toledo province, on 28 October. The regional government says at least 68 people died, and more than 100 were injured. Rescuers worked through the night, and the number of deaths could rise.
The trains, run by Renfe and Iryo, were travelling on the line between Madrid and Seville. The Transport Minister, Óscar Puente, said the control system near Urda failed and six trains were stopped. One was allowed to restart, and it went 25 kilometres before hitting a stopped train. The cause is still being investigated.
The Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, declared three days of official mourning. It is the second deadly high-speed crash in Spain this year.
levels.why: Rail travel depends on trust in safety systems, so the inquiry matters to millions of passengers.

levels.headline: Two fast trains crash in Spain, and at least 68 people die
levels.body:
A terrible train crash happened in Spain on 28 October. Two high-speed trains hit each other near a town called Urda, close to the city of Toledo. At least 68 people died, according to the regional government, and more than 100 were hurt. Rescue teams worked all night, and officials say the number of deaths could rise.
The trains were on the line between Madrid and Seville. The Transport Minister said a computer system that controls the trains stopped working. Six trains were stopped, but one was let go again and later hit another train. People are still looking into what went wrong.
The Prime Minister said there will be three days of national mourning.
levels.why: People need to be able to trust that trains are safe, so officials want to know what went wrong.

levels.headline: Two fast trains crashed in Spain, and many people died
levels.body:
On 28 October, two fast passenger trains hit each other in Spain, near a town called Urda. At least 68 people died, and more than 100 were hurt. Rescue teams worked all night.
The trains were on the line that links the cities of Madrid and Seville. The government says the system that tells trains where to go and when to stop stopped working properly. Six trains were told to stop. One was then told it could go again. It travelled a long way before it hit another train.
People who work on trains and safety are now looking into exactly what went wrong. Spain's leader has said there will be three days of sadness and remembering.
levels.why: Finding out what went wrong can help stop it from happening again.

levels.headline: A very sad train crash in Spain
levels.body:
On 28 October there was a terrible train crash in Spain. Two fast trains hit each other near a town called Urda. At least 68 people died, and more than 100 were hurt. Rescuers worked all night to help.
Trains use signals and computers to know when to stop and go. Spain's government says that the computer system near Urda stopped working. Six trains were told to stop. One was told it could go again, and it hit a stopped train.
Experts are now looking at what went wrong. Spain's leader, Pedro Sánchez, said there will be three days when the whole country remembers the people who died.
levels.why: If we understand what went wrong, we can make trains safer.

levels.headline: A terrible train crash in Spain
levels.body:
Something very sad happened in Spain. Two fast trains crashed into each other on 28 October. Many people died, and many more were hurt. People came to help them all night long.
Trains need signals, a bit like traffic lights, to tell them when to stop and go. Spain's government says the system that controls those signals did not work properly. One train was told it could go when it should not have.
Special experts are now looking at exactly what happened. Spain's leader said the whole country will take three days to remember the people who died.
levels.why: Experts look at what happened so trains can be kept safe.

levels.headline: A sad train crash in Spain
levels.body:
Trains carry lots of people from one place to another. They have to stop and go at the right times. They use signals, a bit like traffic lights, to help them know when. On 28 October, in Spain, two fast trains crashed. This was very sad. Many people lost their lives and many more were hurt.
Grown-ups think the signal system did not work as it should. Special experts are now looking carefully to find out what happened. They want to make sure it never happens again.
The whole country is taking three days to remember the people who died.
levels.why: Grown-ups look into what went wrong so trains can be safer.

levels.headline: A very sad train crash in Spain
levels.body:
When we cross the road, we look for the lights. Trains have lights too. They tell the driver when to stop and when to go. This week in Spain, two fast trains crashed because something may have gone wrong with the signals. Many people died, and many more were hurt.
This is very sad. Helpers, like doctors and firefighters, worked all night to look after people.
Now some clever grown-ups are finding out what happened, so trains can be made safer. The country is also taking three days to remember the people who died.
levels.why: Finding out why it happened helps make trains safer for everyone.

levels.headline: A sad day for trains in Spain
levels.body:
Something very sad happened in Spain. Two fast trains crashed. Many people died, and lots of people were hurt. Helpers such as doctors and firefighters worked all night to look after them.
Trains use signals that work like traffic lights. They tell the driver when to stop and when to go. Grown-ups think the signals may not have worked as they should.
Now clever experts are looking carefully at what happened, so it never happens again. The whole country is taking three days to remember the people who died. It is a time to be gentle and kind to each other.
levels.why: Finding out what went wrong helps keep trains safe for everyone.

headline: Fed holds rates at 3.75% to 4% with two policymakers voting for a rise

terms.meaning: The US central bank, which sets interest rates.
A vote against the majority decision.
An increase in interest rates.

levels.headline: Fed holds rates at 3.75% to 4% with two policymakers voting for a rise
levels.body:
The US Federal Reserve left its main interest rate at 3.75% to 4% on 28 October, as widely expected. Its statement said inflation remains elevated.
Two members of the Federal Open Market Committee dissented. Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack both wanted a quarter-point increase. Cook's dissent stood out because governors rarely vote against the majority, and she had not done so since joining the board in 2022. One economist suggested it might be a protest tied to efforts by the administration to remove her. Hammack also dissented in July.
Markets now price an 85% chance of a quarter-point rise in December, according to CME FedWatch. Chair Kevin Warsh also said that from 2027 the committee will still meet eight times, but one meeting will not include a rate vote.
levels.why: US rates influence borrowing costs worldwide, including for UK mortgages and businesses.

levels.headline: The Fed stands pat, but two dissents point towards a possible December hike
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve held its policy rate at 3.75% to 4% on 28 October. The statement said inflation remained elevated. The decision was widely expected.
Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented, each preferring a quarter-point rise. Governors seldom dissent, and Cook had never done so since taking her seat in 2022. One economist said it could be linked to the administration's attempts to remove her. Hammack also voted no in July, but two other regional presidents who dissented then joined the majority this time.
Markets see about an 85% chance of a December increase. Chair Kevin Warsh said the 2027 calendar will keep eight meetings, one without a rate vote.
levels.why: The path of US interest rates affects markets, currencies and borrowing costs across the world.

levels.headline: US Fed keeps interest rates on hold, with two votes for a rise
levels.body:
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, left interest rates unchanged on 28 October at a range of 3.75% to 4%. It said inflation is still high. The decision was what most people expected.
Two members voted against it. Lisa Cook, a governor, and Beth Hammack, who heads the Cleveland Fed, both wanted a quarter-point rise. Governors rarely vote against the majority, and Cook had not done so before. One economist said it might be a protest linked to attempts by the administration to remove her.
Markets now think there is about an 85% chance of a rate rise in December. The chair, Kevin Warsh, also said that in 2027 one of the eight meetings will not include a vote on rates.
levels.why: Higher US rates can make borrowing more expensive around the world.

levels.headline: The Fed leaves interest rates alone, but some members want them higher
levels.body:
America's central bank, the Federal Reserve, did not change its main interest rate on 28 October. It stays between 3.75% and 4%. The Fed said prices are still rising too fast.
Two of its voting members wanted a small rise of a quarter of a percentage point. They are Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack. It is unusual for one of the Fed's governors, like Cook, to vote against the rest. An expert said it might be linked to attempts by the administration to remove her from her job.
Traders now think there is a high chance, about 85%, that rates will go up in December. The Fed's chair, Kevin Warsh, also announced a change to next year's meetings.
levels.why: What the US does with interest rates affects the cost of borrowing everywhere.

levels.headline: America's central bank keeps interest rates the same, for now
levels.body:
The Federal Reserve, or Fed, is America's central bank. It sets the price of borrowing money, called the interest rate. On 28 October it decided to leave this rate where it is, between 3.75% and 4%. It said prices are still going up too fast.
Two of the people who vote wanted to put the rate up a little. They are Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack. Voting against the others is unusual for Cook, who had never done it before.
People who trade money now think the Fed will raise the rate in December. They think there is about an 85% chance. The Fed's boss, Kevin Warsh, said next year's meetings will be arranged a little differently.
levels.why: When the US changes its rates, borrowing can get more or less expensive elsewhere.

levels.headline: America's money bank keeps the cost of borrowing the same
levels.body:
The Fed is the bank for America's banks. It decides how much it costs to borrow money. This cost is called the interest rate. On 28 October the Fed left the rate where it is, between 3.75% and 4%. The Fed said prices are still rising too quickly.
Of the people who vote, two wanted the rate to go up a little. They are Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack. One of them, Cook, had never voted against the others before.
Many people who watch money closely now think the rate will go up in December. They say there is about an 85% chance.
levels.why: When borrowing costs more, people and companies spend less.

levels.headline: America's bank leaves the cost of borrowing the same
levels.body:
When you borrow money, you pay a bit extra back. That extra bit is called interest. In America, a bank called the Fed sets how big that extra bit should be. On 28 October, the Fed left it as it was.
The Fed has a team of people who vote. Two of them wanted to make borrowing a little more expensive. The rest said no, so it stayed the same.
Some people who study money think the Fed will make borrowing more expensive in December. They say there is a very good chance. It is a bit like a teacher waiting before changing a rule.
levels.why: It affects how much it costs to borrow money in many countries.

levels.headline: America's big bank leaves the price of borrowing alone
levels.body:
Borrowing money is like borrowing a pencil, but you have to give back a little extra. That extra is called interest. A very big bank in America, called the Fed, decides how much extra people pay.
This week, the Fed's team voted to leave it the same. But two of the team wanted to make it go up a little. Most of the team said no.
People who watch money think the Fed might make it go up in December. The big bank says prices are still rising too fast, and raising the extra can help to slow that down.
levels.why: It helps decide how much families and firms pay when they borrow.

levels.headline: America's big bank decides to keep things the same this time
levels.body:
Imagine your teacher has a rule for how much extra you must give back when you borrow a pencil. The rule is about how much extra it costs to borrow money, and America has a big bank that decides it. It is called the Fed.
This week, the Fed's team voted. Most said keep the rule the same. Two said the extra should go up a little, because things are getting more expensive in the shops.
Grown-ups think the rule might change in December. For now, nothing is different.
levels.why: Rules about borrowing money can change what families can afford.

levels.headline: A big bank in America keeps things the same
levels.body:
When you borrow a pencil, you give it back. When grown-ups borrow money, they give back a little extra. The extra is called interest.
In America a very big bank decides how much extra people pay. This week it decided to keep the extra the same. But two people on its team wanted it to go up a little. Most of the team said no.
Some grown-ups think the extra might go up before the end of the year. It is a bit like a teacher thinking about changing a rule. For now, nothing has changed, and everyone is waiting to see.
levels.why: Rules about borrowing money change what families can afford.

headline: UK economy grows 0.1% in August, beating forecasts of a fall

terms.meaning: Gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services a country produces.
Factories, mining, energy and similar industries.
Businesses such as shops, banks and restaurants.

levels.headline: UK economy grows 0.1% in August, beating forecasts of a fall
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August 2026, the Office for National Statistics reported on 15 October. Economists polled by Reuters had expected a 0.1% contraction. July's growth of 0.4% was unrevised.
Real GDP rose 0.7% in the three months to August compared with the three months to May, and CNBC reported annual growth of 2.1% against forecasts of 1.7%. Production grew 0.8% in the month, services were flat and construction fell 0.2%.
Euronews noted that growth came despite a fall in consumer spending. Sterling rose 0.4% against the dollar after the release and gilt yields fell. The figures arrived before the Budget and before the latest inflation data, which showed prices rising faster, so the picture for the Bank of England remains mixed.
levels.why: Growth affects jobs, wages and how much tax the government collects.

levels.headline: August GDP edges up 0.1%, surprising economists who expected a contraction
levels.body:
Monthly GDP grew 0.1% in August 2026, following unrevised growth of 0.4% in July, according to the Office for National Statistics on 15 October. Reuters-polled economists had forecast a 0.1% fall.
Over the three months to August output was 0.7% higher than in the three months to May. CNBC reported year-on-year growth of 2.1%, ahead of the 1.7% forecast. Production rose 0.8%, services were unchanged and construction fell 0.2%.
Consumer spending fell, according to Euronews. Sterling gained 0.4% against the dollar and UK government bond yields dropped. Inflation later rose to 3.5% in September, which keeps the Bank of England under pressure.
levels.why: The data helps decide whether the Bank of England raises interest rates.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew a little in August, when a fall was expected
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August, according to the Office for National Statistics. Experts had expected it to shrink by 0.1%. In July it had grown by 0.4%.
Over the three months to August, the economy was 0.7% bigger than in the three months before. Compared with a year earlier, it grew 2.1%, higher than the 1.7% experts had predicted. Factories, mines and energy producers grew 0.8% in August. Services such as shops and banks did not grow, and construction fell by 0.2%.
The pound rose a little against the dollar after the news, and the cost of government borrowing fell. Shoppers did spend less in the month.
levels.why: A growing economy usually means more jobs and more money for public services.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew slightly in August, beating expectations
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.1% in August. This was better than experts had expected, as they thought it would shrink by 0.1%. The figures come from the Office for National Statistics and were published on 15 October. In July the economy grew by 0.4%.
Over the three months to August, the economy grew by 0.7%. Compared with a year ago, it was 2.1% bigger. Factories and energy firms did well, with 0.8% growth. Services like shops and banks stayed flat, and building work shrank slightly.
Shoppers spent less during the month. The pound rose a little after the news, and the cost of government borrowing went down.
levels.why: It shows whether the country is making more money, which affects jobs and wages.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew a tiny bit in August
levels.body:
The economy is all the things people make, sell and do to earn money. When it grows, it gets bigger. In August the UK economy grew by 0.1%. That is a tiny amount. Experts thought it might shrink, so this was a nice surprise.
The figures come from the Office for National Statistics. It counts how much the country produces. In the three months up to August, the economy grew by 0.7%. Factories and energy firms did well. Shops, banks and other services stayed the same, and building work fell a little.
People did spend less in shops. But the pound rose a little after the news.
levels.why: A growing economy can mean more jobs and more money for things like schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: The UK economy got a tiny bit bigger in August
levels.body:
The economy means all the things a country makes and sells. When more is made and sold, we say the economy has grown. In August the UK economy grew by 0.1%. That is a small amount, like one penny for every £10.
Experts had thought it might shrink, so it was a nice surprise. Factories and energy companies grew the most. Shops, banks and other services stayed the same. Builders did a little less work.
A group called the Office for National Statistics counts all of this. People did spend less in shops. When the economy grows, there can be more jobs.
levels.why: A growing economy can mean more jobs and more money for hospitals and schools.

levels.headline: The UK made and sold a tiny bit more in August
levels.body:
A country makes things and does jobs, such as baking bread, building houses and cutting hair. All of it together is called the economy. When people make and sell more, the economy grows.
In August, the UK economy grew by a small amount, 0.1%. That is about one penny for every £10. Experts thought it might shrink, so this was a pleasant surprise.
Factories and energy firms did best. Builders did a little less work. The shops and other services stayed about the same. People did spend less money in shops that month.
levels.why: A growing economy can bring more jobs and more money for public services.

levels.headline: The UK made a bit more stuff in August
levels.body:
Think about a big bakery. If it bakes more bread this month than last month, it has grown. A whole country can grow in the same way. It is called the economy. It counts everything people make and sell.
In August the UK grew by a tiny amount, about one penny for every £10. Experts thought the country might make less, so this was a nice surprise. Factories and power companies were busy. Builders had a bit less to do.
People spent less in shops. When a country grows, there can be more jobs and more money for schools.
levels.why: A growing country can bring more jobs and better public services.

levels.headline: The UK economy grew a tiny bit
levels.body:
Imagine your school has a cake sale each month. If you sell a bit more cake this month than last month, your sale has grown. A country can grow like that too. We call everything people make and sell the economy.
In August the UK grew just a tiny amount. Grown-ups thought it might shrink a little, so this was a nice surprise. Factories were busy, but builders were a bit quieter.
When the economy grows, there can be more jobs and more money to pay for things like schools and parks.
levels.why: More growth can mean more jobs and money for schools and hospitals.

levels.headline: The country made a tiny bit more than before
levels.body:
Imagine your class sells cakes every month. If you sell a few more this month than last month, your sale has grown. A country can grow too. Everything its people make and sell is called the economy.
In August the UK grew by a very tiny amount. Grown-ups had thought it might shrink a little, so this was a nice surprise. Factories were busy, but builders were a bit quieter.
When a country grows, there can be more jobs. There can also be more money to pay for things everyone shares, like schools, parks and hospitals.
levels.why: Growth can bring more jobs and more money for things everyone shares.

headline: Germany and Japan agree to deepen cooperation on economic security and technology

terms.meaning: Protecting a country's supplies, technology and trade from outside pressure.
Minerals used in electronics, electric cars and wind turbines.
Trade run on agreed international rules rather than power or threats.

levels.headline: Germany and Japan agree to deepen cooperation on economic security and technology
levels.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi agreed in Tokyo on 28 October to deepen cooperation on economic security and high technology. Euronews reports they issued joint statements on both subjects and welcomed a joint declaration of intent on critical raw materials.
The two countries plan to broaden supply sources and improve substitutes for rare earths in their car industries. They will also set up a high-level dialogue on artificial intelligence and work together on defence against cyberattacks. The statements stressed the importance of peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait. China and the United States were not named, but the message appeared to criticise both indirectly.
At an economic forum in Tokyo, Merz called for a new political alliance to strengthen rules-based global trade.
levels.why: Closer ties between two big economies could change supply chains for cars, chips and minerals.

levels.headline: Merz and Takaichi pledge closer work on economic security, rare earths and AI
levels.body:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi met in Tokyo on 28 October and agreed to deepen cooperation on economic security and high technology, Euronews reported. They issued joint statements and welcomed a declaration of intent on critical raw materials.
They plan to widen the supply base for rare earths and make them easier to substitute in both countries' car industries. A high-level dialogue on artificial intelligence will be set up, and the two will work more closely on cyber protection. The statements highlighted peace in the Taiwan Strait. Neither China nor the US was named, but the wording seemed to criticise both indirectly.
Merz also urged a new alliance to defend rules-based trade.
levels.why: It shows how major economies are reducing reliance on single suppliers.

levels.headline: Germany and Japan agree to work more closely on technology and supplies
levels.body:
The leaders of Germany and Japan, Friedrich Merz and Sanae Takaichi, met in Tokyo on 28 October. They agreed to work more closely on economic security and advanced technology. They published joint statements and welcomed a declaration about critical raw materials.
They want to find more places to get rare earths, which are minerals used in car parts and electronics, and make them easier to replace. They will also start a high-level dialogue on artificial intelligence and cooperate on protecting against cyberattacks. The statements said that peace in the Taiwan Strait is important. They did not name China or the US, but seemed to criticise both indirectly.
Merz called for a new alliance to protect trade based on rules.
levels.why: It could affect the supply of the materials behind cars, phones and green energy.

levels.headline: Germany and Japan team up on technology and key materials
levels.body:
The leaders of Germany and Japan met in Tokyo on 28 October. They are Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. They agreed to work more closely together to keep their economies secure and to share advanced technology.
One focus is rare earths. These are minerals used in car parts and electronics, and the two countries want to depend less on a small number of suppliers. They will also talk regularly about artificial intelligence and work together to fight cyberattacks. Their statements said peace around Taiwan matters. They did not name China or the US, though the message seemed aimed at both.
Merz also asked for a new group of countries to support trade that follows agreed rules.
levels.why: The deal shows that countries want safer supplies of the materials they rely on.

levels.headline: Germany and Japan promise to work together on technology and key materials
levels.body:
