The leaders of Germany and Japan met in Tokyo on 28 October. They are Friedrich Merz and Sanae Takaichi. They agreed to work together more on keeping their economies safe and on new technology.
Part of this is about rare earths. These are special minerals that are used to make car parts and electronics. At the moment only a few places can supply a lot of them. The two countries want more choice. They also plan regular talks about artificial intelligence, which is computer software that can learn, and about stopping cyberattacks, which are attacks on computers.
Merz also asked for countries to agree on fair rules for trade.
levels.why: Countries that depend on one supplier can be hurt if that supplier stops selling.

levels.headline: Germany and Japan agree to be better friends in trade and technology
levels.body:
Germany and Japan are two countries that make lots of cars and machines. Their leaders met in Tokyo on 28 October. They are Friedrich Merz and Sanae Takaichi. They agreed to work together more.
One plan is about rare earths. These are special minerals needed for phones, electric cars and other machines. Right now a few places supply most of them. Germany and Japan want to find more places to buy them from. They also plan to talk about artificial intelligence, which means smart computer programs, and to protect against hackers.
Merz said countries should agree on fair rules for trading with each other.
levels.why: If one place stops selling, other places need another choice.

levels.headline: Germany and Japan agree to help each other with trade and technology
levels.body:
Germany and Japan are countries that make lots of cars, machines and gadgets. On 28 October their leaders met in a city called Tokyo. They are Friedrich Merz and Sanae Takaichi. They agreed to help each other more.
They talked about special minerals used to make phones and electric cars. Only a few places have much of these minerals. The two countries want to find more places to get them. They will also talk about smart computer programs, called artificial intelligence, and about how to stop hackers.
One leader said countries should trade fairly, with rules everyone agrees on.
levels.why: Having more than one supplier makes it less risky to depend on others.

levels.headline: Two countries agree to help each other more
levels.body:
Germany and Japan are two countries far apart from each other. On 28 October their leaders met in Tokyo. They said they would work more closely together, a bit like two friends who decide to share their toys.
They talked about special minerals that are used to make phones and electric cars. If you only have one shop that sells something, you are in trouble if it closes. So they want more places to get these minerals. They will also talk about smart computers and about hackers.
One of the leaders said that all countries should play fair when they trade.
levels.why: It is safer to have more than one place to get the things you need.

levels.headline: Two countries say they will be better friends
levels.body:
Imagine you need a special pencil, and only one shop sells it. If that shop shuts, you are stuck. It is safer if there are lots of shops. Countries think about this too.
Germany and Japan are two countries that make a lot of cars and machines. Their leaders met on 28 October and agreed to work more closely together. They want to find more places to buy the special things that machines and phones need. They also want to talk about smart computers and how to stop hackers.
One of the leaders also said that everyone should follow fair rules when they trade, like in a good game.
levels.why: Having more choices keeps countries and families safer.

levels.headline: Two countries say they will help each other
levels.body:
Imagine you need a special crayon, and only one shop sells it. If that shop shuts, you are stuck. It would be safer to have lots of shops.
Countries worry about this too. Germany and Japan make lots of cars and machines. They need special minerals for them, and only a few places have much of them.
So their leaders met and promised to help each other find more places to buy things from. They also said they will talk about clever computers and about stopping hackers. It is a bit like two friends who agree to share and to look after each other.
levels.why: Having more than one place to get things makes countries safer.

headline: US campaign finance filing system goes offline days before the midterms after a reported hack

terms.meaning: The Federal Election Commission, the US body that oversees campaign finance.
US elections held halfway through a president's term.
Money raised and spent to influence elections.

levels.headline: US campaign finance filing system goes offline days before the midterms after a reported hack
levels.body:
The Federal Election Commission's electronic filing system has been down since about 10pm ET on Monday 26 October, and the agency says it was targeted by a hacker or hackers, CNBC reported on 28 October, citing an email obtained by Reuters.
An FEC official told compliance firms that a "bad actor" was trying to breach its systems, so public-facing services were shut. The agency said it had identified the problem and was applying a fix, but the system was still offline early Wednesday. It has not said who was responsible, whether anyone got in, or whether data was compromised.
Previously filed reports remain searchable, but new time-sensitive disclosures are blocked. These normally fall within 24 to 48 hours in the last 20 days before an election, which is 3 November. The FEC has had only two members since October 2025, fewer than the four needed to take official action.
levels.why: Voters rely on these filings to see who is paying to influence elections.

levels.headline: FEC filing outage blocks campaign finance disclosures days before the midterms
levels.body:
The Federal Election Commission's online filing system has been offline since about 10pm ET on Monday 26 October, with the agency saying hackers targeted it. CNBC cited an email seen by Reuters.
An official told compliance firms that a "bad actor" tried to breach the systems, and public-facing services were shut down. On Tuesday night the FEC said it had found the problem and was putting a fix in place, but the system remained down early Wednesday. It has not said who was behind it, whether anyone got in, or whether data was affected.
Older filings can still be searched, but new time-sensitive disclosures cannot be filed. In the last 20 days before the 3 November midterms they are normally due within 24 to 48 hours, while outside spending is rising. The FEC has only two members, so it cannot take official action.
levels.why: It could delay public information about election spending at a sensitive moment.

levels.headline: A reported hack takes the US campaign finance filing system offline before the midterms
levels.body:
The US Federal Election Commission, which oversees election money, says its online filing system has been down since about 10pm Eastern time on Monday 26 October. The agency says it was targeted by a hacker or hackers, according to CNBC, which cited an email seen by Reuters.
An official told firms that help campaigns file reports that a "bad actor" had tried to break into its systems, so it closed its public services. The FEC said it had found the problem and was fixing it, but the system was still down on Wednesday morning. It has not said who was responsible or whether any data was taken.
Older reports can still be searched. New reports, which are normally due within 24 to 48 hours near an election, cannot be filed. The midterms are on 3 November.
levels.why: People use these reports to see who is paying for political campaigns.

levels.headline: US election money reporting system goes offline after a suspected hack
levels.body:
The US body that watches over election money, the Federal Election Commission, has a website where campaigns report who gives them money and how they spend it. That system went offline at about 10pm on Monday 26 October. The agency says hackers targeted it.
An official told companies that help campaigns that a "bad actor" had tried to break in, so the agency closed its public services. It said it had found the problem and was working on a fix, but it was still down on Wednesday morning. It has not said who did it or whether any information was taken.
Older reports can still be searched. Newer ones cannot be sent in. This matters because elections are on 3 November, and campaigns must report quickly in the last weeks.
levels.why: It makes it harder for voters to see who is paying for political campaigns.

levels.headline: A website where US campaigns report their money has been knocked offline
levels.body:
In America, people who run for office raise money. They must tell the public where it comes from and how they spend it. A government body called the Federal Election Commission, or FEC, runs a website for these reports. That website stopped working on Monday 26 October.
The FEC says hackers, which are people who break into computers, tried to attack it. It shut parts of its website to stay safe. It says it found the problem and is fixing it. It has not said who did it or whether any information was stolen.
Old reports can still be read. New ones cannot be sent in. Elections happen on 3 November, so the timing is awkward.
levels.why: People want to know who is paying for campaigns before they vote.

levels.headline: A US government website for election money has stopped working
levels.body:
When people want to win an election, they often ask for money to pay for posters and adverts. In America, they must report who gave them money. A government group called the FEC keeps a website for these reports. The website stopped working on Monday 26 October.
The FEC says hackers, people who try to break into computers, may have attacked it. It closed some of its website to keep it safe. It says it knows what the problem is and is trying to fix it. It does not yet know, or has not said, who did it.
Old reports can still be read, but new ones cannot be added. America has important elections on 3 November.
levels.why: People want to see who pays for campaigns before they vote.

levels.headline: A website for American election money has broken
levels.body:
In America, people who want to win an election often ask others for money. They must tell everyone where the money came from. They do this using a special website. This website belongs to a government group called the FEC.
On Monday 26 October, that website stopped working. The FEC says computer hackers tried to break into it. Hackers are people who try to get into computers where they are not allowed. The FEC closed some of the website to stay safe and says it is working on a fix.
Old reports can still be read, but new ones cannot be added. Important elections are on 3 November.
levels.why: Voters like to know who is paying for campaigns.

levels.headline: A computer problem stops people sharing election money details
levels.body:
In America, people who want to win an election raise money. They have to tell everyone where it came from, like showing your homework. They use a special website for this. A government group called the FEC looks after the website.
The website stopped working on Monday. The FEC thinks hackers, who are people who try to break into computers, tried to get in. The FEC closed some of the website to keep it safe. Now it is trying to fix it.
Old reports can still be read, but new ones cannot go on. Big elections are coming on 3 November, so people want it fixed soon.
levels.why: People should be able to see where election money comes from.

levels.headline: A computer problem stops a website from working
levels.body:
Imagine your class is choosing a class captain. The people who want to win give out posters, and they must tell everyone who paid for them. That keeps things fair. America has a special website for this, which belongs to a group called the FEC.
The website stopped working this week. The FEC thinks computer hackers tried to break in. Hackers are people who try to get into computers where they should not. The FEC shut some of its website to keep it safe, and now it is trying to fix it.
Big elections are coming on 3 November, so people want it working again soon.
levels.why: Elections are fairer when everyone can see who is paying.

levels.headline: A computer problem has stopped a website from working
levels.body:
Imagine your class is choosing a captain. Children who want the job make posters, and they must say who paid for them. That keeps the vote fair. In America there is a special website where people tell everyone where their election money came from.
This week the website stopped working. Grown-ups think hackers may have tried to get in. Hackers are people who try to get into computers where they are not allowed.
The people in charge shut some of the website to keep it safe, and now they are fixing it. Big elections are coming soon, so everyone hopes it is mended quickly.
levels.why: People can vote more fairly when they can see who is paying for campaigns.
